utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those following our proceedings. Before the witness will be brought in, I would like to raise some procedural matters. You will have noticed that the Chamber issued this morning a Scheduling Order setting dead-lines for the final briefs and for end dates for the final oral submissions. In relation to that, I would like, on behalf of the Chamber, like to inform the parties that the Chamber doesn't intend to call any Chamber witnesses. Therefore, I take it that this witness and the next witness, who is waiting, will be the last witnesses in this trial. I see Mr. Vanderpuye nodding. I come to another question I would like to raise. The Chamber intends to hold a housekeeping session next week to deal with the documents on the marked-for-identification list, and any other pending housekeeping matters. The Chamber hereby requests that the Court Officer circulate an updated MFI list to the parties by tomorrow for purposes of preparing for this housekeeping session. For the housekeeping session, the Chamber requests that the parties update the Chamber on the status of any pending translations; and if translations are still pending, provide dates of when they can be expected. With respect to all other MFI documents - and there are quite some - on the list, the Chamber requests the parties to be ready to make submissions in court regarding their admission. I would like to discuss with the parties when they will be in a position to make these submissions orally in court, that means when we should schedule this housekeeping session. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence suggests that we do this on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Prosecution; will you be in a position to make your oral submissions on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate your patience. Any time Tuesday or Wednesday would be fine for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic. Mr. Gajic, the Prosecutor is proposing Tuesday or Wednesday. Would that be convenient for you, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Defence has certain commitments and we have to plan our journey to Belgrade, but we would welcome Tuesday. It is acceptable to us, obviously, if the Prosecution is unable to submit their submissions on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tuesday is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are currently scheduled for 9.00 on Tuesday next week, and all other sessions will then be cancelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But, of course, we don't know if we need this session tomorrow. And I would kindly invite the parties to make proposals for an agenda for that housekeeping session. If there are any matters to be raised during that housekeeping session, we would welcome these proposals for the agenda by tomorrow. This is all what I wanted to raise before the witness will come to the courtroom. Mr. Vanderpuye, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I just have a bit of information for the Chamber regarding Exhibit 562B. P562B. There was an error made, and the incorrect document was uploaded, which is described as a 19 July 1995 intercept at 2116 hours. In fact, it should be dated 15 July. I have it backwards. The correct intercept is 19 July and what was uploaded was the 15th of July. And we have also replaced the document with the correct -- with the correct version. The document that's in e-court is 03205338 through 5340. The correct document is 03205538 through 5540.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please check the transcript. Is a correction necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it should be 03205538 through 5540. And we would like to replace the document with the Court's permission. We haven't done that yet, but we would like to, because of the error, to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, it was already communicated yesterday to the Chamber and we appreciate this correction. Leave is granted to change the attachment, and the Registrar will do his job to replace the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, pursuant to Chamber's order with regard to Exhibit D365 marked for identification, the Defence has uploaded two articles from the book --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Gajic please repeat the title and the author of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And please repeat the title of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title of the book is "The Srebrenica Massacre: Evidence, Context, and Politics."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. The Chamber will consider this information and take the necessary steps. Anything else before the witness will enter the courtroom? The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Skrbic. Welcome back, again. Again I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his re-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Greetings to all present. Peace be upon this house and I would like the outcome of this trial to be decided by providence and God's will and not according to my wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I also would like to greet Mr. Skrbic and to wish him a pleasant stay in our midst. Mr. Skrbic, yesterday we saw a document in which we saw that one individual was buried at Kazani according to the statements given by the commander and the witnesses who appeared before the court to establish his death. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: (redacted) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A DNA analysis of any individual that disappeared and it is not yet known whether this person got killed or was executed can only be conducted after the remains of the individual are found, samples taken to the laboratory, and an analysis performed. Therefore, before doing any DNA analysis, an exhumation of the individual in question has to be carried out and a sample taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you please tell us, is it necessary to identify an individual that had already been identified and buried, and if there are witnesses who confirmed that he was killed in action and not executed and we have a confirmation of this fact from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a person is buried, then this person is buried under his or her full name and with other personal details. They are also buried in line with the customs of the people that this individual belonged to. So this person cannot be treated as a missing person or a person who disappeared, but, rather, a person who had died in the way that was proven and provided in the course of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Please, since we are talking here about different methods of establishing the facts, can we look at D316 now, which is a judge's report. (redacted) (redacted) Now, can you tell me this: Can the time of death be reliably established through a DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether a DNA analysis can establish the time of death as well. But I do know that once a person is buried, there is no need to conduct any DNA analysis because this person was buried under his real name in accordance with the peoples' customs. In this particular instance, this was done at the request of the deceased's family. The relevant court issued a ruling declaring this person dead so that his family can claim certain benefits enshrined in the law with regard to fallen combatants during the war. So if there is no such request from the family, even a court cannot declare a person dead. Once this happens, then this person is removed from the missing persons list and is no longer registered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have D166 in e-court, page 595. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, what we see here is what Witness Jean Ruez talked about, and this is a section from the transcript where his words are recorded, and I'm going to read it. I am reading from line 8 to line 17. [As read] "This area has been processed in 1996 by a team of expert from Finland who were operating in that area in 1996, totally disconnected from our activities, they were collecting surface remains. But it's important to note that 600 bodies have been collected in that area. These are bodies of victims killed in combat, in ambushes, in shelling, and possibly also in other circumstances which are impossible to sort out between -- I mean, for us, at least, between combat and other situations." My question is: Have you perhaps heard about the information that 600 individuals from the area of Bare had been executed in the way described by Ruez and that their surface remains were found? This is what he stated when he gave evidence in the General Krstic's trial.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard about this particular incident, but I have read one of the statements given by Mr. Ruez. As far as I remember, he gave this statement or this evidence during a hearing before the representatives of the French parliament. In addition, I can confirm that Mr. Ruez said at the time -- and I would really like to give you a verbatim quotation, because it is very difficult to repeat it without referring to the exact quote. I'm going to quote the relevant part of Mr. Ruez's statement. "At this moment, some 20 secondary mass graves remain to be exhumed. We know precisely the position and locations of all of those mass graves. For each and every one of them, the contents have been verified. This means that in each and every of these mass graves we have found mortal remains of several persons, their numbers ranging from 80 to 100 bodies. Most probably, the total number of those persons is over 4.000. We can say that they were killed in cold blood during that systemic and organised process." This is page 5 of Mr. Ruez's statement, number 40307456. When I read this relevant portion of his statement, I asked myself: How is it possible that somebody can claim that bodies were found in the graves that were not exhumed; and if those graves were not exhumed, how is it possible to see almost an exact number of bodies? As regards your question, in this portion of Mr. Ruez's statement I can confirm that the agency for research and documentation from Tuzla described the chronology of events surrounding Srebrenica. And in that chronology, inter alia, it says that a majority of the bodies were exhumed from the territory where combat had taken place during the breakthrough of the 28th Division. Several bodies from the mass graves -- and then they go on to list the mass graves, the same one as can be found in the indictment, Lazete, Cerska, Branjevo, and let me not go on enumerating them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, for the sake of the record, please can you tell us to whom this statement of Mr. Ruez was made, and when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement was provided on the 28th of February, 2001 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction: 22nd February, 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, the statement was provided to the parliamentary commission of the French parliament. In any case, it was given on the 22nd of February, 2001. I'm sure of that. And I gave you the ERN number of the first page, which is 40307456.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Relying on the ERN number provided by the witness, I can say for the record that this is Exhibit D40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Yesterday you spoke about the victims, the remains, and the Prosecutor even showed you the remains that were found in those mass graves, and you have just told us that some people talk about things that cannot be seen. We asked Mr. Manning to confirm what Mr. Ruez said, and Dean Manning was one of the witnesses in these proceedings. His words were recorded on page 12-- 10219. I quote what he said. A question put to Mr. Manning was this: "Do you know --" we can't see it yet. "Do you know where the mortal remains were buried, in which grave?" He answered: "I was not involved in the process. I can say that the surface remains were collected and were kept for a number of years in Tuzla, in the salt mine, in the tunnels that had been used as a salt mine." My question is this: Mr. Skrbic, does this point to the fact that the bodies and the mortal remains were transported to the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know anything about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I came across such information. Let me just mention the article entitled "The Icon of Srebrenica." We already quoted from that article. In this article it is mentioned inter alia that before 1998 thousands upon thousands of bodies were collected from all over Bosnia and they were brought to Tuzla airport and that's where DNA analysis took place. What you have just read out confirms that. I'm also aware of that information. Besides, I would like to say that the commission of the Government of Republika Srpska in its own report stated that the commission of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina for missing persons is only -- the only body authorised to deal with exhumation of Bosnian and Croatian victims and that the commission of the Government of Republika Srpska handed over all the necessary documents about mass graves to the commission of the federation. The way I see things, the exhumation commissions could not have had such a strict authority. When I say "strict authority," what do I mean? I mean that it was not possible that only one commission - and that was the one from the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina - to be authorised to deal with exhumations. I believe that it is fair and it is only logical for those commissions to be of a mixed composition. Those commissions should have had representatives of all the three peoples as their members, and exhumations should have been carried out in the presence of international bodies in order to avoid all possible speculations with regard to the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the last word has just been corrected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sometimes we have to be patient. Mr. Tolimir, please carry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Prosecutor asked you whether you studied Janc's report, Dusan Janc's report. The question was put to you on page 33; do you remember that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shown a lengthy report on 7.000 exhumed and identified bodies. I don't remember that anything else was shown to me. I already shared my position on that with you. I said that I didn't see what period that list applied to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That is what the Prosecutor asked you about. Do you know that the author of that collective report put all the victims in the report without making any distinction between those that were killed in combat and those that were possibly executed? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If General Tolimir is referring to the report written by Mr. Janc, I would appreciate it if he could give us a cite to that particular point. My recollection of that report is that it clearly distinguishes between surface remains and bodies or remains recovered from mass graves, several of them. And in the methodology of that report, it explains which surface remains he considers are associated with the events of Srebrenica and which he considers that are not associated with those events. So if General Tolimir has a particular point with respect to what distinction there is made, if any, between combat casualties and non-combat casualties, it would be helpful if he could put that on the record so that we can identify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you give a reference for your statement, page 12, lines 4 through 7, which was included in your question put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. When he presented his report on the 26th of May, 2011, on page 14679, Dusan Janc said, on lines 16 to 23, and I quote: I would say that most of the people, if not all the victims found in the mass graves were crime victims; they had been executed. However, not all surface remains were result of combat. We know that some of them were killed and left on the surface and that's where they were found. Some of them had comitted suicide, which means that they were not combat casualties, so we can't say that all the 688 surface victims were also combat victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Now you have heard the position of the author of that report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you will have realised that this is quite distinct from what you put to the witness first. I would appreciate if you would put these observations or quotations literally to the witness. Please carry on and put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm reading the first sentence: I would say that most of the people, if not all of them, i.e., all of the victims found in the mass graves were crime victims. They had been executed. Please, how do you understand this sentence, Mr. Skrbic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please have this part of the transcript on the screen. We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up transcript page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] I think the Court Officer is working on that. In the meantime, the witness is invited to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it can be claimed for all the victims that they were executed and that they were crime victims only if it has been established really precisely what the cause of their death was, whether the death was forcible death after they were disarmed and captured or in some other way. Before those details are revealed, in my view, it is not possible to claim that crimes were comitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You will remember the Bare report that also concerned the sixth person. I'm reading the second sentence from Janc's report. He says: "Not all the surface remains were a result of combat." How do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is contained precisely in my previous answer. This means that the bodies that were found on the surface had lost their lives in various ways. Some were killed in combat, some were killed in inner fighting, some may have comitted suicide. They could have died in any other way, but this has to be established with a great deal of precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this, Mr. Skrbic: If this was not established precisely, through exhumations, is it then proper for experts who compiled collective reports to claim the nature of death of those people, i.e., what kind of deaths they suffered?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless proper identification is carried out commensurate with the applicable standards, primarily by conducting a DNA analysis - although I said I'm not very familiar with it - it is impossible to claim that the cause of death has been established. Only after the cause of death was established, then one can say whether the death was caused by a criminal act or some other act.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And I quote the next sentence: "We know that some of them were killed and were left lying on the ground where they were found." My question is: When you studied the material relating to Srebrenica, did you come across anyone's statement about people being killed and left lying on the ground? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, at the beginning of my testimony I said that I did not explore the issue of victims and how they became victims. All I managed to find about this matter was of superficial nature, and I use it only for the purpose of trying to prove the exact number of Muslim survivors according to the methodology that I had chosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. And I am quoting the last sentence, which says: "Some of them comitted suicide, which means that not all the 688 persons whose remains were found on the surface were killed in combat." Now, my question is: How many victims were found on the surface? Is it the number that is quoted in Mr. Janc's report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate if we can define the notion of a victim, and let us be a little more precise in doing so, because it is a wide notion. In my report, I used terms such as "executed" and "killed," and I did not use the term "victims" because even a live person can be a victim. In this specific instance that you're asking me about concerning the number of those found on the surface, it is obvious from the statement of this gentleman that it is impossible to state with any degree of accuracy how many of that number were executed, how many were killed, how many comitted suicide, how many killed each other, and so on and so forth, and most probably this will never be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, in this consolidated report, if only 688 individuals are considered as surface remains, does that reflect the reality in view of the statements that you made reference to in your report and in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not entirely sure what General Tolimir means when he says that 688 individuals are considered as surface remains. Mr. Janc's report deals with DNA-identified individuals, and I'm not sure if that's the context in which General Tolimir is putting the question. But the numbers that Mr. Janc talks about in his report specifically deal with DNA-identified individuals. So if General Tolimir is referring to the total number of surface remains recovered, then that's something -- that's a different question than what he's put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Tolimir, you can rephrase your question or please give a reference where Mr. Janc is mentioning 688 individuals considered as surface remains.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to give the reference now. And I quote the last sentence. He says: "Some of them comitted suicide and were not participating in combat ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And was it taken from the transcript or from a report, or what you are quoting from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading the evidence given by Mr. Janc from the transcript which says that: Therefore we cannot say that all the 688 surface remains belonged to the people who were killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, based on this sentence, can we conclude that all the victims mentioned in his report whose remains were found on the surface were killed in combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, this gentleman is talking about the victims found on the surface and that here he is talking about the number of the victims found on the surface, and it is about them that he says that it is impossible to reliably establish the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. If 600 people were found at Bare alone, is it possible, then, that only 88 people were found in the area near Srebrenica where the breakthrough was carried out as we heard of those who witnessed this breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have the same objection. And perhaps it will be of assistance to General Tolimir if he were to review P170, Annex B, paragraph 2, on page 2, and that might help him frame his questions more accurately in terms of Mr. Janc's testimony and also the conclusions in his report. I can read that into the record if it will be of assistance, but perhaps it will be better for Mr. Gajic to assist General Tolimir in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. It is up to the Defence how to deal with these matters, but of course we all would appreciate, I assume, to have the relevant parts of documents on the screen so that we can follow what you are reading, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the portion that refers to surface remains is P170, page 43, in English. It speaks about 688 surface remains that were identified out of the total number of 961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have that page in English on the screen. We need it in B/C/S, too. What is the page in B/C/S? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find it shortly, Your Honour. Mr. President, it's page 60, 6-0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it you are now referring to the second paragraph in both languages. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was speaking about the 688 victims who were identified. We cannot talk about those who haven't been identified. The total number of surface remains is 961.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Is it possible that only 300 were found on the surface outside the area of Bare given that 600 surface remains were found in Bare?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either I didn't understand the question correctly or, since I am looking at this document for the first time, I cannot give a precise answer because I was unable to fully understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to rephrase it. The document relating to Mr. Ruez where we read his statement that in Bare 600 people were found and taken to Tuzla and that was done independently from the team lead by Mr. Ruez. Now Mr. Janc, in the report referred to by Mr. Vanderpuye, Mr. Janc says that 961 surface remains were found, of which 688 were identified. My question is: Does this figure include only those found by Mr. Janc, whereas those 600 remains from Bare have not been taken into account?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that I was able to understand your question now, here they are talking about 688 identified persons of which 600 were found in Bare. Eighty-eight persons had been to be found elsewhere and not in Bare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, just to understand your answer: How do you know that 600 out of 688 are found in Bare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a minute ago General Tolimir said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But it's not your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I see this document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on the next page of this document that's now in e-court, Mr. Janc has actually set out in detail specifically where these identified surface remains were recovered. It would be helpful, obviously, to put that to the witness to see if it conforms with his understanding of the events, as General Tolimir has asked him about it, rather than for him to speculate on where these particular surface remains referred to in Mr. Janc's report come from. It's just a matter of flipping the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would it assist you if we go to the next page in both the languages?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case let's go to the next in both languages. If that is the correct page and you want to put a question to the witness in relation to that, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we can see here the names of the locations where surface remains were found. Can you see anywhere the name of Bare?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't managed to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that Mr. Janc did not analyse the location of Bare in his report at all since he made no reference to it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If he made no reference to it, that means that he did not analyse it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it yet another indicator of the fact that it is better to find how many people survived instead of using the number of deaths?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is better to have information from various sources and quarters, because they can be collated and confirmed as to their accuracy, and then on that basis it is possible to conclude how many people were killed in combat or in some other way and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, is it possible for -- that the OTP investigation team disregarded the 600 surface remains found in Bare and that they were never put to you yesterday during cross-examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information relating to the number of people either killed or executed must be presented and must be taken into consideration with a view to arriving at a final number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have in e-court D38. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, it's an interesting statement you now made. "All the information relating to the number of people either killed or executed must be presented and must be taken into consideration with a view to arriving at a final number." Did you do that with your report? I mean, to take all information into account, especially about killed and found dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took into account all the information regarding Muslim survivors because that was my methodology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just said: All the information relating to the number of people either killed or executed must be taken into account to arrive at a final number. You didn't do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever information I had about the number of killed and executed that I found in the indictment, all that I took into account when I did my calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, carry on please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's look at a document that we called up before the Presiding Judge put his question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see a document in front of you. Its author is Mr. Tokaca; I'm sure you heard of him. In the article he says, We found 500 survivors who were registered as missing. He is the director of AID in Sarajevo. He stated that in Banja Luka he appealed to everybody with information about survivors, and then I am quoting: [As read] "... regardless of their nationality or religious affiliation who are listed as missing were called to inform all the relevant authorities IDC or others in order for this information to be registered if they are not reported." This is the reporting agency. And the report was provided on the 31st of March, 2010, and I quote: "The biggest problem --" I am quoting from Tokaca's words: "'The biggest problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina is a perfidious monopoly on information.'" Tokaca has said -- pointing out that the IDC wanted to break this monopoly by compiling the Bosnian crime atlas. My question is this: Did you ever see Tokaca's report before? And if you did, can you perhaps explain what he meant when he said "perfidious monopoly on information"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an occasion to see this document before. When it comes to perfidious monopolies, I really don't know what he meant. In this case this is in quotation marks which means that Mr. Tokaca did not want to go into much detail. This is my opinion. If he didn't -- if he wanted to be very explicit, he would not have left the term under quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the last paragraph, where it says: "'In the course of our research project on the loss of life, we discovered some 500 people from Srebrenica who were still alive. We also have information that just over 7.000 persons were killed in the area, but not all of them were from Srebrenica. There were inhabitants from Vlasenica, Zvornik, Bratunac, Visegrad, and Rogatica, and this is also seen in the fact that we registered 70 people who were buried at the Potocari memorial centre but who didn't perish in Srebrenica.'" And he also said: "We also found 500 inhabitants of Srebrenica who were alive, and -- although they were listed as missing." Could this information about 500 people from Srebrenica who were found alive, could it prove that they were put on the list of missing persons as it is stated in here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We've actually seen this document a couple of times during the course of the trial, and I think General Tolimir is well aware that subsequent to this report that Mr. Tokaca gave a statement saying that he was misquoted and that this statement was taken out of context. It is P1370. I think it's only fair, to the extent that General Tolimir is aware that Mr. Tokaca effectively retracted his statement, or the statement that's attributed to him in this article, that he put that to the witness in framing the question. Otherwise it's misleading to the witness and is going to result in a distortion of the record before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the document number, the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe it's P1370, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, are you able to rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, the 500 missing people from Srebrenica, were they found alive according to Mr. Tokaca? What do you know about that? Because you hail from the region where this piece of news circulated for a long time.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm what is written here. I am familiar with that. I don't know anything else with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at D369.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's confidential and should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at the first page of this report, which shouldn't be broadcast according to the Presiding Judge, although I don't see any logic in that, but we shall see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This page can't be confidential.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D368 is a public version of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you should use the public redacted version for showing it to the witness. It's much better. Then there is no need to prevent broadcasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Tolimir has just mentioned a number and it has been properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see a table from your expert report and it is entitled: "The Movement of Prisoners from Srebrenica." Tell us, please, did you also include the numbers available to the Prosecution about the -- of those who were killed or/and who went missing in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table shows those who were taken prisoner from the 28th Division and it is based on the data and on Mr. Butler's statement. He was an OTP expert witness. It is also based on this trial, the ongoing trial, and also from case IT-05-88-PT, which means that I have been able to list the paragraphs from each of these documents, including Mr. Butler's report as well as case IT-05-88/2-1 and this case which is currently ongoing. Nothing else has been included in the table but the prisoners who are referred to in the three documents that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up page 3 in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am reading the last sentence which begins with the number -- this is the fourth paragraph that starts with "the maximum taken prisoner," and it starts with "... the number 3.820 equals 4.420 (4.820)." "According to the debriefing (attachment 4, their source being the UNHCR 28 July 1995, page 2)." This is your reference. "3.000 from the column were taken prisoner in total, but according to the document from the Tuzla agency for investigation and documentation (AID) a few thousand were taken prisoner from the column which was breaking through." Thank you. My question is this: Did you try to cover up the information available to the OTP on the number of those who were killed or went missing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't try to cover up anything. On the contrary. I copied word for word all the information from the documents that I referred to. I didn't skip a single piece of information, a single number. And in the meantime, I came across the information from the AID in Tuzla, which was the overview of prisoners and those who were killed based on their information. I wanted to do my own comparison and to see that information taken from various sources that I did not skip a single bit of information. I did not attempt to cover up anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. If we look at the last paragraph on this page, you drew Mr. Vanderpuye's attention to what is written here during his examination-in-chief when you said that you established that those who were killed in Konjevic Polje and Kravica were taken into account twice. Can you explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber? I apologise, Sandici and Kravica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly what General Tolimir is referring to in the cross-examination which gives rise to this line of re-direct examination. If he can provide me with a cite, that would be helpful. But I don't think that there was anything specific to the issue that he's just asked the witness about or, frankly, for this chart that we see in front of us which was covered on direct examination to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you give us a reference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness wants to answer, he may answer, otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I take note of Mr. Vanderpuye's objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not a question for the witness, if he wants to answer or not. If you put a question, he has to answer. But the Prosecutor asked you if you would be able to provide with the reference to his cross-examination. Can you give us a reference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could find the reference but it would take time. I would have to search all of my notes. Maybe I will do it during the break. But now let's look at the last paragraph -- that's why I'm saying that I'm taking notes of Mr. Vanderpuye's objection. I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The last paragraph on the page that we have before us says: "If we keep in mind the fact that the captured soldiers from the 28th Division of the BiH Army shown in the meadow in Sandici village (1.000) were in the meadow temporarily and were transferred to Novo Kasaba, then the number of prisoners shown in Novo Kasaba also includes those shown in Sandici meadow." My question is this: Can you please tell us, Mr. Skrbic, what did you mean by this? Are things really the way they are described here or not? My question is this, actually: Those who were killed or, rather, who went missing in Kasaba, were they presented together as those who were killed and went missing in Sandici? Do they form the same group? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I am referring to in here is a -- listed under the ERN number of the first page. This is a document issued by the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army. This is a report to the General Staff of the BiH Army where they speak about information that they received from the state security service in Tuzla, after the interrogation of two men who had escaped from the meadow in Sandici. During the interrogation, they stated that about a thousand of them had been in the meadow, that they had been there only temporarily, and that within a short space of time they had been transferred first to Kravica and then, also within a short space of time, to Novo Kasaba. This sheds new light, i.e., puts things in a different perspective. This means that the two figures referring to Novo Kasaba also encompass the 1.000, so they cannot be added to each other because the figure of 2500 to 3000 also encompasses the number of 1.000 according to the statements of the witnesses who had provided their statements to the state security service in Tuzla. This is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please take a look at document PD5/46.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The document that was shown to you did day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A document with this number doesn't exist. Please repeat the correct number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I repeat the number: P95--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Once again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P95, page 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It can't be the right number. Please check again. P95 is the pseudonym sheet of a ... and it's under seal. Mr. Tolimir, please give the right number now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I had information that that was the number of the photograph taken in Sandici and that's why I quoted it in that way. My apologies. And Aleksandar will try to figure it out. In the meantime, we can proceed with other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, we should stop here. We are just before the break. And before we have the break, I will shortly raise another matter. Mr. Gajic, you indicated that the -- you have uploaded parts of the 65 ter document 1D1103 as a separate document which contains the foreword of a book and one of the articles. This was uploaded as 1D1120 and which now can be assigned as D365. That was your request from the beginning of today's session. We must have our first break now. I hope that the question of correct numbers of exhibits can be resolved during the break. We will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I hope you were able to sort out the reference you asked for and the right exhibit number. You have the floor. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have found the proper number. It should be P94. So can we please have P94 in e-court. As for the reference that you asked me for, I haven't looked for it because it simply slipped my mind. But if I manage to find it, I am going to quote it. Can we now see page 46 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you have been shown this and then later on in a document relating to Borovcanin one can see that around 1500 Muslim soldiers were taken prisoner in Sandici. Now, please, can one conclude exactly how many soldiers are depicted in this photograph below the line where the buses are parked? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact figure about how many people there are in this group, but it is obviously a small group, probably fewer than 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the house across the road towards right, can we say that the size or the surface of this house is larger than the size of the group of people shown in this satellite image?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am able to estimate, the size of this house is slightly smaller than the area where these people are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now hear what one of the eye-witnesses said about this group of people and this location. We have seen that this picture was taken on the 13th of July at 1400 hours. And this is what --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the closed session because I'm going to quote the words of a witness who testified in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, when showing this document to you, the Prosecutor quoted the penultimate paragraph, which reads that: [As read] "On the night between the 12th and 13th of July, 1500 men were taken prisoner and there were more than 200 dead." Now, my question is: According to this report about the number of the death [as interpreted], can one say that these deaths were caused by combat or by some other means? What can one conclude on the basis of this combat report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can conclude on the basis of such combat report that there was fighting between members of the 28th Division of the BH Army and this police unit of Republika Srpska, and that in the course of that fighting 20 -- 200 members of the 28th Division were killed and that the remaining soldiers surrendered after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Now, please, in this Prosecution document is it clearly stated that in fighting that lasted several hours and during the attack on Konjevic Polje which continued today the enemy had more than 200 dead? In your opinion, these 200, do they need to be counted as victims or as troops killed in action?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These men were killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now take a look at the last paragraph, and I quote: "According to all indications, the number of Muslim soldiers who did not manage to break through is on the rise and is approximately between 5.000 and 6.000, which means that we have intense combat ahead of us. I hope that we will successfully carry out this task also." Now, please, in this last paragraph, is this commander only making assumptions or does he have indication of the fact that 5- or 6.000 soldiers haven't been able to make a breakthrough yet? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this information means that the 28th Division was still in the process of breaking through and that they were to proceed with it further. Also, the information that this police commander has to the effect that another 5- or 6.000 are preparing to break through must have been obtained in the course of interrogation of those who had already been taken prisoner or in another way. I cannot precisely confirm the source of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now thank you. Is this information speaking about the 5- or 6.000 who still have to break through or were they captured or did they still have to fight this number of men? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's talking about the soldiers who carried on with the breakthrough and he anticipates further clashes with them to take place in the forthcoming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, please, can we now have P1769. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This document was shown to you yesterday, and we see the information about the enemy. In paragraph 1, I quote: "A large enemy group was infiltrated in the region of Pobudje Brdo and the region of Konjevic Polje. Units of the 5th Engineering Battalion and the MUP successfully resisted the enemy. About 1.000 to 1500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed." My question is this: Could the officer in charge be able to report about this situation directly or did he have to receive reports and information from both locations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the standard military procedure and as far as I can know, this is how things were done in the Army of Republika Srpska. Regular combat reports arrive from subordinated units. Then they are processed. And then executive summaries are then compiled for the superiors. And from the Main Staff -- and then from the Main Staff they are sent to the Supreme Commander. This is the procedure applied to regular combat reports and I know that that procedure was followed by the Army of Republika Srpska as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The commander of the unit, the superior officer, was a witness here. He spoke about this document, P1769. And he said -- he answered a question, that is. On page 9439 of the transcript, lines 10 through 16. The date was 7 February 2011. Thank you. I quote what he said on page 9439, lines 10 through 16, to the Prosecutor's question, What did you learn about what was happening in the area? he answered: [As read] "We learnt what is contained in the report. A group of soldiers of the BiH Army from Srebrenica was moving through the region. Some of them had already been unable to walk, so we didn't know what the situation was. We tried to deal with the situation as best as we could, providing support to our own barracks, bearing in mind the number of men that we had at our disposal, and that number was very low at the time." Did you know that he also stated that at that location that he spoke about, his unit was deployed and provided support for the materiel and technical equipment that the unit had at that location? Thank you. I don't want to read everything.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I am not aware of that. Let me explain: All witness statements that were taken here in this case were not known to me. I was not familiar with all the statements that were taken in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I stopped you because you were overlapping. Now your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you don't know what was stated by the witness, we are going to quote what he said on page 9467, line 21, through page 9468, line 4. "Q. Do you believe ... that 1.000 to 1.500 people were killed, as stated in this paragraph?" And the witness answered: "I can't either believe or disbelieve this. [As read] "This was more of information to a -- to the superior command telling them what we had learned. And then they can go on and undertake certain measures in order to check this information because we didn't have an intelligence organ or any other person who would be qualified to check this information. If we had known that, then we would have probably told them where they were and what they were doing." My question is this: I have just read out a part of the witness's testimony - can you conclude based on what I have just read that this commander compiled his document based on the information available to him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All commanders draft their combat reports based on the information they received from inferior -- subordinated units or other information received from flanking units, units that act in concert. In other words, no combat report can be compiled if there is no prior information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now let's see what he said on page 9473, lines 15 through 24, to a question by the Presiding Judge: [As read] "Who is the author of paragraph number 1, entitled 'Enemy'?" The witness answered: [As read] "I don't know. It must have been the staff sergeant who wrote this, most probably, based on what he heard, because all of us heard about that in Konjevic Polje, you know, people were talking about that. People were talking about certain problems. They were saying that there were some people who were killed, some captured. And most probably he wrote all that in order to draw attention to this, because there were very few of us in the barracks. We were not safe. Things were going on around us and we didn't know what was happening." My question: Is it clear from the second paragraph that this report was drafted based on second-hand knowledge? I don't want to call it rumours. How reliable is this report, then?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one would conclude that based on his statement, based on the statement of this witness or this witness's testimony. It seems that a staff sergeant drafted paragraph 1 based on the information that he had. I can't confirm that because I don't know how they drafted their reports - what information, what data about the enemy they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we assume that what the witness said in answer to the Presiding Judge's question was true, what would be the degree of the reliability of the information contained in this report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There's two issues that arise from this: The first is that obviously the witness has already answered the question in terms of his ability to assess the reliability of this report. The second thing is that he goes well beyond the scope of the cross-examination in this case. This document, as with other documents of a similar nature, were put to this witness to determine whether or not he himself had examined these documents prior to drafting his report. His answer on almost every single occasion was that he had not reviewed them and he was not familiar with them at that time. It does not go to the reliable of the report itself; it goes to what the witness was aware of and what the witness relied on in drafting his own report. So to the extent that General Tolimir wants to question on -- on these documents, it seems to me that for that to be responsive to the cross-examination of this witness, it has to be within the context of what this witness knew in relation to his report, as opposed to his general impressions about the documents that he's now seeing essentially for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your response to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. What we are seeing is that the document is not relevant, and the witness could not take it into account when he made his calculation. And the question was whether he actually saw this document ever. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this question was already answered during the cross-examination. He didn't see that and he didn't take it into account. But Mr. Vanderpuye put another objection to you, that now you are dealing with a separate issue, namely, what the interpretation of the content of this document, unknown to the witness prior to his testimony here, would be. And he was not asked during cross-examination about that. What is your position, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The question was whether the expert was familiar with this information. I am trying to get the answer from the witness as to the relevance of the information for an expert report by any expert, including yourself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness has clearly explained during his whole testimony that he didn't know these documents, that he didn't take them into account because they were not relevant for that -- his method of calculation. What do you want to gain from him in re-examination which should relate to the content of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you don't allow it, he doesn't have to answer the question. My question was whether, if he had known about it, whether he would have taken it into account as a relevant document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This question was already answered by the witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I'd like to call up P176, page 104. P11-- P1776, page 104 in Serbian, 97 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We now see it. And I have to tell you that this is a table taken from Mr. Brunborg's report. The title of the table is: "220 cases with inconsistent date of death, disappearance between the 2005 OTP list of Srebrenica missing and ABiH records." Thank you. My question is this: Does this type of information call for the re-examination of the number of dead and missing during the events surrounding Srebrenica, i.e. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this document shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- does this type of information -- and I repeat my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document should not be broadcast. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I repeat my question: Does this type of documents with inconsistent data about the cause of death for 220 persons, as well as the date of deaths, call for the re-examination of information using the methodology that you yourself used; i.e., following the number of survivors? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a number of persons appears with different sets of data about their cause of death or disappearance or any other such information, this points to the fact that the information is not reliable and cannot be used as evidence on what had happened, whether people were killed, whether they died or went missing, or anything else. So when an inconsistency is established, it shows that the data is not reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you now explain: What is the degree of reliability of records on the killed and missing army members? And I'm calling for your experience when answering this question.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. The degree of reliability is a hundred per cent. There is precise information about every soldier who is injured, killed, or who has gone missing. Moreover, based on such data information, administrative procedures are started by the families in order to seek proof of death in order to obtain some legal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Yesterday the Prosecutor put several questions to you, and he put his case to you about the removal of the civilian population from Srebrenica. Within that context, he showed you an intercept, on page 19166 of the transcript. Let us now see one of the so-called Srebrenica videos.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P991 is the exhibit number. And I would like to play it from 46 minutes, 24 seconds, to 48 minutes, 33 seconds. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We stopped at 48 minutes, 33 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Kindly tell us: Based on this video-clip that you saw, who requested that the civilian population leave Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the interpreter saying that the BH command in Sarajevo requested that population to be relocated. That's how I understood the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at the beginning of the conversation hear what General Mladic asked Mr. Karremans? If not we can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I wasn't able to hear a good part of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we replay the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you try to make out what Mr. Mladic said. He wasn't interpreted into Serbian because he was speaking Serbian, so probably the interpretation was into English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see P991 again, starting from 46 minutes, so that we may hear what General Mladic said to Karremans.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped at 46 minutes, 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you now hear what General Mladic said to Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard him ask, "What do you want?" He asked Colonel Karremans to say what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation. We don't receive interpretation, perhaps because the microphone is off. Once again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we replay it but without an overlap between what Mladic and Karremans are saying and my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted the video-clip to be replayed from the beginning of the conversation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was stopped at 46 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was stopped at 46 minutes, 36 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I repeat my question: Did you hear what General Mladic said to Mr. Karremans? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really heard him ask, "What do you want? Tell me what you want now." That's really all I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear who had asked for the meeting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, obviously you have a problem with listening to the video-clip, maybe turning up the volume or turning it down, because it could clearly be heard what General Mladic said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Usher please assist, and I kindly ask the technician to return to the beginning of the clip so we can replay it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If General Tolimir has a particular proposition to put to the witness regarding what's on the tape, I don't see any harm in him putting the proposition to the witness. The tape speaks for itself. It's not necessary for the witness to actually hear it if everyone else knows what's on it. He can simply put the question to the witness and ask him, Based on this ... and represent what's on the tape, and put his question. I think that will speed things along and it wouldn't be necessary for -- for -- it wouldn't be necessary to go through the trouble of trying to sort out the technical difficulties with the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, did you have a problem with the microphone or the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I had problems. I switched to channel 4 instead of channel 6. Thank you. But I understood the last part of Mr. Vanderpuye's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Essentially -- essentially, Mr. Vanderpuye said it's not necessary to play this video again because we all know what is taped and said there, if the witness is not able to hear that. Just put your question to the witness. That was the proposal of Mr. Vanderpuye. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, if you heard the part where he said, "You requested a meeting," tell us who it was who requested a meeting and what was -- what were the words of Mr. Karremans when he spoke about the relocation of the population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the meetings between the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS and Colonel Karremans, the commander of DutchBat. I know about that from documents. And I know that they took place at Bratunac at the Fontana Hotel. I also know that there were three such meetings. I know about all that from documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know who requested the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot provide a precise answer to that question because I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could we play it again so we can hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I -- you don't -- you don't have the floor at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You don't have the floor at the moment, Mr. Tolimir. I help you to figure out this problem. The second question: Do you remember or do you know the words of Mr. Karremans when he spoke about the relocation of the population. Do you know that, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was able to catch was when Colonel Karremans mentioned the BH command in Sarajevo, and as far as I understood, that command wanted the population to move out. That's what I heard. I really cannot give you a reliable answer and state with certainty that I heard this or that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you got the answer. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here is my question: Did you hear General Mladic say, "What do you want? You requested a meeting"? Did you hear it or didn't you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the question "What do you want?" but I didn't understand the rest of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Mladic silent, then, and did Karremans answer the question "What do you want?"

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, Colonel Karremans continued his story, and the interpreter interpreted for General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The witness didn't hear everything, but what can we do? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In July 1995 they signed an agreement about the relocation of the Srebrenica population. It was signed by Rajko Kusic, Hamdija Torlak, Semjon Dudnjik, and Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see that agreement. D51 is the exhibit number. We saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn the volume down?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the agreement signed by the persons whose name I have just said. I am interested in item 7 of the agreement, which reads - I quote: "In accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and the Additional Protocols of 1977, the civilian population of Zepa shall be given the freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." Here is my question: Please explain what this language means, "freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 7 is very precisely phrased and cannot be misinterpreted. It clearly means that the population of Zepa has the opportunity to choose where they want to reside temporarily as long as the hostilities are going on. And this temporary quality is a consequence or is determined by the hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document P1434. Thank you. Thank you, e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye yesterday read out to you a document of the 28th in which -- or which said that if -- if the Muslims fail to honour the agreement, do not register the refugees --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: do not -- the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- we'll keep them for an exchange. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That was written on the 29th. And here we see a cable dated 30 July. It says, "Information about prisoners of war in Rogatica holding centre." And we see names from 1 through 45. We can also look at the following page. There's a list of all prisoners of war from the Zepa area. Here is my question: In this cable, did they act as had been said before? Do you know from documents that the Muslims left that territory on the 30th and did not surrender as they were supposed to under the agreement that we saw a minute ago? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first answer your question about this telegram. It is clearly shown here that the prisoners had been registered and sent to the Rogatica camp together with the list. Now, as for your second question, can you please repeat this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that this was written in the telegram dated 27th of July and that already on the 30th, after the Muslims had left the area, all the prisoners had been properly recorded one day later?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clearly shown here that everyone who was taken prisoner was registered on the 30th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 3 of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here you can see, under C, the last paragraph, entitled: "Treatment of r/z," and I quote. It's page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
