utterances.text: Indeed. We should move to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote: [As read] "Pursuant to the orders of General Tolimir and his instructions, all the necessary measures are taken and in accordance with the possibility they are mainly being carried out. Among other things, the following was done: [As read] "Categorisation of war prisoner was done and they are placed in three rooms." I repeat: [As read] "The categorisation of war prisoners was done and they are placed in three rooms. The healthy in one room, the wounded and the sick in another room, and the member of the former leadership in the third room. "'Atlantida' is separated and placed at another location and has better accommodation. "The Effendi is allowed to pray in the room five times a day. "They have food. "They can use an outhouse. "They have medical treatment. "On the 30th of July of this year, the prisoners of war were visited and registered by the ICRC delegation office at Pale." My question is: Were all prisoners of war in Zepa registered by the International Committee of the Red Cross, the ones that are shown in the list that you saw?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the prisoners of war who were taken to the Rogatica camp were visited by the International Committee of the Red Cross, Pale office, and were registered at the Rogatica camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are these instructions in keeping with the international laws of war and other covenants that regulate and provide for the treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They were treated fairly, as the document shows. Had it been possible to give them a better treatment, this would have been probably done, but it was done according to the available capabilities at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at P122.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was the document shown to you by the Prosecutor. We see in the heading that it was drafted on the 29th of July, one day prior to their registration. I am going to quote the last sentence of the third paragraph, which reads: "The persons taken before cease-fire should not be registered and not be declared to the international organisations. We are going to keep them for an exchange in the event of the Muslims not honouring the agreement or if they make a breakthrough from our encirclement." My question is: Was it possible to do anything with regard to the prisoners of war in one day only?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the procedures that have to do with humanitarian situation while combat operations are in progress can be carried out only when the tactical situation allows it. That is the view from the military doctrine. Once the tactical situation allows this, then procedures are being initiated, including those relating to humanitarian issues and issues relating to prisoners of war. Now let me add one thing: The only officer who is authorised, who has the powers and the right to assess the tactical situation and to give his forecast of the future development is the commander of the unit, and it is to be done on the basis of the information he receives from his services.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am reading the continuation of this same paragraph. "We are going to keep them for exchange in case the Muslims do not honour the agreement or they manage to break through from the encirclement." My question is: Based on the documents that you reviewed, do you know if the Muslims accepted the exchange all-for-all as envisaged in the agreement, or did they break through from our encirclement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I frankly don't see what this is responsive to in the cross-examination. Presented this document to the witness during the cross-examination and asked him, quite plainly, What do you make of it? And that had to do with the registration of the prisoners. I don't see what the last question is that General Tolimir just asked has to do with the nature of that examination. And perhaps he can provide some sort of basis for it, but I don't see any apparent connection between the nature of the cross-examination and this line of direct -- re-direct examination. The second thing is: Since General Tolimir has represented at least twice in the last couple of minutes that all of the prisoners on the list that we saw relating to the Rogatica prison were registered, I would like to know whether it's his position that Atlantida, number 45 on that list, who we know in this trial to be Avdo Palic, was among those prisoners that was registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Vanderpuye raised two questions. What is your position to that? Not two questions, two objections. Please give us your position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye posed a question whether it was not customary to register the prisoners of war, and that's what he asked the witness to answer, and that's why I put my question whether an exchange of all-for-all was being carried through or did they manage to break through the encirclement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you explain that a bit further? I don't see the connection between registering prisoners of war and carrying out an all-for-all exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If there is an exchange all-for-all, then the numbers are irrelevant. Every side will give as many prisoners as they have. There will be no registration. However, if there is an exchange to be made, then reciprocity has to be observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to the witness. Can you tell us if there is any legal requirement for not registering prisoners of war who were kept and prepared for an exchange of prisoners of war with the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if there is such a legal provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, carry on please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, was the exchange to be carried out with the number there of prisoners that was kept for the prisoners from the Zepa Brigade that were in captivity elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an exchange of prisoners is agreed on the principle all-for-all, that means, number one, that the agreement should be honoured; and number two, that neither side should hide the prisoners that they have, but hand over all the prisoners that they have. And that applies to both sides. They have to hand over all the prisoners that they had in custody at the moment when the agreement went into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Thank you for having testified in this courtroom. Thank you for having come to The Hague. I wish to thank you on behalf of the Defence. I wish you good health, and I wish you God-speed in your future life and work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is only one question left. This is the admission of four documents. I have the -- I formed the impression that you want to raise this, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That is one of the things I'd planned to raise. The other thing I wanted to raise, and it is a rather extraordinary circumstance, is the opportunity to re-cross-examine this witness on a specific issue. And that relates to a document that he was shown yesterday as concerns an individual. I think we were in private session so I won't mention his name, but it was an individual who had been allegedly killed on the 7th of July, buried on the 8th of July, and that his wife apparently had sought a certificate or a declaration from the court in Lukavac concerning that death. I do have specific -- very specific evidence on that issue, which was not the subject of cross-examination, and it is a single document with respect to that. I anticipate -- and in fact I can probably do it without asking the witness a question. I would simply tender the document, if that would be a better way to go about it. But it is directly responsive to that specific issue that was raised by General Tolimir on his re-examination outside the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is the position of the Defence to this request for continuing cross-examination on this specific matter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence doesn't know what the whole thing is about. However, if this will be of help to the Trial Chamber, we do not object to the admission of any document. And I would actually like to thank Mr. Vanderpuye for proposing to tender into evidence yet another document, with your leave of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, the Chamber grants your request, but only specifically to this document you referred to. And you may put a question in relation to that or not. But after that, Mr. Tolimir will have the opportunity to put a question too in relation to that specific document. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. 65 ter 7620, I would be requesting leave to add it to the Prosecution's exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it, again, that Mr. Tolimir has no objection to that, to add this document to the list. I take it from his last comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you. No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No objection. You may proceed, and leave is granted to add it to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Maybe we can have it up in e-court. I apologise, it does not have a translation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm showing you, Mr. Skrbic, is the part of the autopsy report --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go into private session, I think I can make this a little bit easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7620 shall be assigned Exhibit P2877. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you so wish, you may put questions to the witness in relation to that document we just received.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you remember, did I ask you yesterday at the end of the day whether it was possible for the body to have been transported from Kazani to Lazete, since the corps command also confirmed that the body was buried in Kazani? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. And I also remember what I answered to that. I answered that if what you had shown me was authentic - and one can tell from the document that the document is authentic - that it is then possible that the gentleman who had been killed was exhumed and then his body was transferred to the mass grave in Lazete, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, what is your final position in relation to the two reports in confidential versions and the public redacted versions? Mr. Tolimir has tendered these reports, then your position was to receive them preliminarily, and that was the reason why we marked them for identification. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm happy to share with you my position with respect to the admissibility of these reports. I don't know that I -- actually, I don't know whether or not it would be appropriate to do that in front of the witness. I don't know if he will have to be re-called, or not, in respect of the application. I would ask, therefore, that he be excused or dismissed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- as would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the presence of the witness in that respect is not necessary. Sir, after a long time, after several days of testimony, now you are released from court. You may go home to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for your expertise you were able to provide, your knowledge, and we wish you all the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, we have just considered a possible need to call you back into the courtroom after having dealt with your expert report. There may be any reason to discuss something or to put a question to you in that respect. Please bear with us a bit and wait for several minutes in the waiting room. In principle you are released, but may be re-called. Please wait some minutes and you will give notice -- you will get notice if you can go home or have you to come back to the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. President. With respect to the admissibility of the reports tendered by General Tolimir: As concerns the military report, which is D366 public and D367, we have no particular objection to the Court receiving that report in evidence. Mr. Skrbic was a member of the military, he was -- he received education in military matters and affairs, and we're confident that on the record and in light of his testimony the Trial Chamber will attach the appropriate weight to that report, having reviewed his neutrality, or lack thereof, the reliability of that report, or lack thereof, and the objectivity with which it was presented, both in his testimony and as a written document. However, with respect to Mr. Skrbic's report on the movement of the Srebrenica population, which is D368, the public version, and D369, our position is that that document is simply not admissible as expert evidence in this case. It is fundamentally and in its essence a demographic study of the population of Srebrenica, and I think Mr. Skrbic was quite clear in his testimony as regards to his qualifications to make such an analysis. First, and you will recall, Mr. President, that you questioned him to some extent on his CV, and it was clear from his CV not only that he did not have any substantial publications in the area or expertise -- area of expertise that would be required to render an expert report, a demographic analysis of the population of Srebrenica, but it was also readily apparent from the nature and the extent of his education in that matter, whereby he indicated that he didn't have any advanced degree in statistics, demography, mathematical statistics, or any other discipline that was specifically related to the subject matter that was -- of his report. There are two things that Mr. Skrbic said which I think are also dispositive of the issue. First thing he said was, obviously, that he didn't have a degree that was directly related to the nature of the report that he prepared concerning the Srebrenica population. The second thing that he said - and I think this is probably the most significant thing - is that his report didn't require that he have any such skill, knowledge, or training in order to examine those issues. What he said, in effect, was -- and I think I have it here at page 19036 of the transcript -- is in response to my question: "And it's the case that your expert report on the population of Srebrenica actually didn't require any advanced degree or special training in any of those subjects?" He said: "That's right. The calculations were very simple, because I had at my disposal finalised facts and information. And anyone who knows the basics of mathematics would be able to do that provided they invest some effort into it." This precisely undermines his expertise or purported expertise in the subject matter of that report. What his -- his expert status requires that he be able to render assistance to the Trial Chamber in its understanding or analysis of issues in dispute in this case based upon his specific training, knowledge, or expertise in the subject matter on which those subjects arise. And he's essentially said, Not only don't I have it, but it's not required. In effect, General Tolimir could have simply put in the documents that this witness testified about and relied on the Trial Chamber the draw the same inferences, if that be the case, as this witness came up with, and it wouldn't require anything special. It wouldn't require any special skills. It wouldn't require anything but a little bit of effort, which is what the witness said. And I think on that basis the report patently does not satisfy the standard for expert evidence in this Tribunal. I would also point out that he was questioned rather extensively on the methodology that he employed in producing this population report, and it's very clear from his answers that what Mr. Skrbic did in this case was he essentially relied on a methodology of convenience. He relied on a methodology which was calculated to support a conclusion that he had already drawn before he began the study. And we know this because he produced a paper, he produced a book, and then he incorporated the paper and the book essentially as the basis, the fundamental basis, of the report that he submitted here -- that General Tolimir, rather, has submitted here for the Trial Chamber's analysis. He shared with us the motivations that he had to produce that book, which forms the substance of the -- of the report that General Tolimir is tendering. He said first and foremost what motivated him to study this matter was that he could not accept that officers in arms with him would engage in the kinds of acts that are alleged in the indictment. That was the first thing. The second thing was that he said that he was essentially tired of being bombarded with this so-called official version of what happened in Srebrenica "without anybody proving it." Mr. Skrbic prepared this report because he had a very clear agenda in mind in preparing it. This is why it's clear that he did not take into account any of the prisoners - any prisoners - in this case that he knew to be in VRS custody. He said it, and General Tolimir demonstrated that he was aware that there were prisoners in VRS custody in the report. But as a question of comparing the totals of the population before the fall of Srebrenica and after the fall of Srebrenica, somehow that figure, however it is that he came to know about it, managed to be excluded from his result. And then he reached the conclusion, therefore, that not but a few hundred people could have been the potential victims of this crime, when he's listed over 4.000, as alleged in the indictment, in the very beginning of his paper, and he has failed to account for all of the prisoners, as I demonstrated during the cross-examination, in terms of tallying the total of that population.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: By engaging in a pattern of systematically excluding relevant evidence to determine the issue which was the subject matter of that report, he has rendered that report utterly worthless and unreliable as expert evidence in this -- before this Tribunal. As any evidence before this Tribunal. Rule 89 requires that evidence meet the minimum threshold of reliability before it's even admissible. In this case you have clear evidence that the conclusions that Mr. Skrbic arrived at, he arrived at as part of a carefully designed methodology to substantiate conclusions that he knew were in conflict with the evidence that he had at his disposal, which is the evidence of prisoners - and thousands of them, by the way - in VRS custody. I would suggest that to the extent that the Trial Chamber may be inclined to receive his report in evidence in this case, it should not be received as expert evidence because it doesn't fall within the definition of the rules regarding the same. And, frankly, to the extent that it comes in at all, it should be to put in context his inexpert analysis, his bias, the length to which he will go to manipulate the information he has to achieve a given result, and put in context the rest of his testimony in this case. But for no other purpose. To be frank, Mr. President and Your Honours, Mr. Skrbic's population report that has been offered by General Tolimir in this case should not have the imprimatur of this Tribunal. It's an affront, frankly. It's an affront to the victims of these crimes and it's an affront to the integrity of these proceedings. On that basis, we respectfully request that it be excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, do you intend to respond?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am not sure if we have enough time to finish this before the break, because we are now 15 minutes beyond the break time. We will ask the Court Officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you can put that, your position, on the table -- on the record in two minutes or three minutes, because we have only five minutes left and we have to decide if we will release the witness. First Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a clarification for Mr. Vanderpuye. You are saying on that basis, with respect to the request that it be excluded, you want it to be excluded as an expert report or you want it to be excluded completely? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want it to be excluded completely. And to the extent that the Trial Chamber may be inclined to admit it, I would suggest that it not be admitted on the basis as an expert report, certainly, and on the basis to place in context, as I mentioned before, his bias, his inexpertness, so the Trial Chamber can evaluate the rest of his testimony, if it's admitted at all. But I would submit that it shouldn't be admitted at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do the parties think that the witness can be of any assistance further, or should we release him?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think he can be of further assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't mind him being released. We will just present our position just like Mr. Vanderpuye did, but we will do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We should do that after the break. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness should be released now. And we must have our second break. I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir if that is a good idea to release the next witness, too, and to commence the examination of that witness tomorrow morning. What do you think, after this lengthy day, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that would be the most appropriate attitude towards the witness. He's been here all day, he's been waiting. He must be tired, himself, so he should be released. And the same happened yesterday and then again today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will do that in that way. We must have our break now. We will come back perhaps in 20 minutes, 6.25, and then we want to hear from you, your position in relation to these expert reports. And after that we will adjourn and take all these arguments into consideration. We adjourn and resume 5 minutes -- 25 minutes before -- I am tired, too. 25 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor to tell us your position in relation to these reports.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, as far as the motives are concerned: Although the report is based on the paper and the book - as pointed out by the Prosecutor - it does not diminish its significance. It means that he spent some time analysing this problem. Secondly, the witness has studied military documents that pertains to the movement of survivors and he derived an answer based on that, or, rather, a calculation, without denying the crimes. Thirdly, this kind of analysis indicates what one should focus upon when analysing the problems relating to Srebrenica during the war. The fact that the witness did not rely on documents relating to prisoners and executions does not diminish the value of his analysis because the purpose of this analysis was not to show how many people died and whether the proposition about the 7.000 or more victims are sustainable. During his education, the witness studied the methodology of establishing the number of losses in a war. He doesn't have to attend civilian schools to be able to do that. Therefore, he is educated and skilled enough to produce an analysis that demonstrates military losses. The fact that the OTP does not accept his report cannot be the reason for it not being admitted into evidence. It is up to the Trial Chamber, when the time comes, to evaluate its reliability and to what extent the Chamber can rely upon it when rendering its judgement and ruling. We are not talking about the entire analysis of those who were killed or executed after the fall of Srebrenica. This is a partial analysis that deserves to be taken into consideration. With regard to what was said about this witness being biased, I would like to say that he said, "I do not deny that crimes were comitted," and he expressed his views without proffering any conclusions about the number of those who were killed or executed. He also underlined that he did not take into account a single fact that was not established and confirmed by relevant organs and institutions as being in the public domain and true. This particularly refers to the list of survivors published after the fall of Srebrenica, and that was the subject of his analysis. Anyway, all the answers and all the questions boil down to how many people survived. If you know how many people survived, then you know who the killers are.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: then you know the number of the losses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence would just like to add that this witness cannot be qualified as being biased because he relied on the document of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the United Nations and he did not use at all any documents from the Army of Republika Srpska and the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, the Chamber noted that the Prosecution didn't object to the admission of the report in relation to military areas. This is D366 and D367 under seal. This report and two versions will be received as exhibits. In relation to the other report, "Movement of the Population of Srebrenica," we have heard substantial submissions by both parties. Many arguments were put to the Chamber. The Chamber would like to take the liberty of considering all what was put to the Chamber, and we will postpone a decision. We have in mind to deliver a decision on that during our housekeeping session next Tuesday so that we can give you, then, our response to that. In my view, this concludes the hearing of today. We adjourn. And we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom to hear the last witness. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of February, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
